blogs.title: Fair use in the gig economy: Second Circuit greenlights late-night mockery of Cameo videos
blogs.description: This post unpacks the court’s factor-by-factor fair use analysis and explains why Kimmel’s broadcast of Santos’s Cameo clips qualified as transformative commentary. It highlights the court’s reliance on a reasonable observer standard after Warhol, its dismissal of bad-faith arguments in light of Google v. Oracle, and its market-harm framing that focuses on substitution rather than reputational damage. It situates the ruling alongside Hachette and Authors Guild as part of a trend toward robust protection for critical and comedic reuse of publicly distributed short-form content.

blogs.title: From Harper and Row to Google v. Oracle: Bad faith keeps shrinking in fair use
blogs.description: This post examines the court’s treatment of deception in acquiring the works—Kimmel’s use of fictitious names—as irrelevant to the fair use inquiry. It traces the doctrinal arc from Harper and Row’s good-faith dictum to the Supreme Court’s skepticism in Google v. Oracle and shows how the Second Circuit reads that skepticism into modern fair use. The post explores implications for journalism, satire, and undercover stings, and where courts might still credit bad faith (e.g., where the deception aims to supplant a licensing market rather than facilitate commentary).

blogs.title: Pleading-stage fair use is now a feature, not a bug
blogs.description: Focusing on procedure, this post analyzes the court’s comfort resolving fair use at Rule 12(b)(6) by examining the videos and broadcast segments themselves. It compares TCA Television, Cariou, and Hachette, and explains how judicial notice of copyright registrations and the works’ content allows early dismissal. The post offers practical guidance for media defendants on building a record for motion-to-dismiss wins and flags the limits—when factual disputes about market substitution or unpublished status could still warrant discovery.

blogs.title: Can platform terms rescue creators from fair use? Santos’s contract theories run aground
blogs.description: This post dissects the state-law claims, emphasizing why the Cameo Terms of Service could not be enforced by Santos under Illinois’s strong presumption against third-party beneficiaries, and why an implied-in-fact contract failed under New York law for lack of essential terms and a meeting of the minds. It discusses how platforms might draft clearer third-party beneficiary provisions and creator-facing protections, and the unresolved preemption question lurking beneath the court’s merits-based dismissal.

blogs.title: Market harm in the meme era: Why mockery does not substitute
blogs.description: Zeroing in on factor four, this post explains the court’s conclusion that Kimmel’s use did not usurp the Cameo market because criticism and lampooning are not plausible licensing substitutes under Campbell and Hachette. It probes whether there exists a cognizable licensing market for rebroadcasting paid shout-outs and why courts generally exclude a rights holder’s claimed market for authorizing criticism. The post considers potential edge cases, like wholesale compilation or systematic rebroadcasts that might approach substitution.

blogs.title: No harm, no fraud: The out-of-pocket rule as a shield in prank litigation
blogs.description: This post analyzes the dismissal of Santos’s fraudulent inducement claim under New York’s out-of-pocket damages rule (Lama Holding; Connaughton). It explains the narrow pathway for fraud claims in media-prank contexts where the plaintiff cannot show actual pecuniary loss beyond the benefit of the bargain. The piece explores alternative pleading strategies plaintiffs might consider, and why reputational or expectation harms are unlikely to suffice absent quantifiable losses.

blogs.title: The missing publicity claim and the newsworthiness backstop
blogs.description: Noting what was not litigated, this post explores the conspicuous absence of a right-of-publicity claim and assesses how such a claim would likely fare given New York’s strong newsworthiness and commentary protections for matters of public interest—especially when a public figure monetizes personalized speech. It considers preemption risks and the overlap between fair use’s transformative analysis and the First Amendment defenses that typically doom publicity claims in satirical broadcast segments.
